evidence: Retained. In the satellite, r1 is asphalt between a dark longitudinal seam (its left polygon edge) and the thick solid white separator; the stop bar crosses it. The near and mid forward views show the matching lane: a wide unmarked left lane between the solid yellow median-edge line (about 0.5 m from the granite median kerb) and the solid white separator. The dark seam runs on straight through the crosswalk past the median nose, so it is not the median edge. The real lane continues about 1.3-1.5 m left of the polygon to the yellow line, so r1 under-covers this lane but is the same facility. In the mid view this lane looks at least as wide as the right lane, consistent with that extra width.
binding: No arrow or word marking is visible in this lane anywhere between the mid camera (about 50 m) and the stop bar in the near view (about 28 m), and none in the sunlit satellite part. The adjacent r2 is marked 'ONLY' with a right-turn arrow, and the road continues straight across the junction, so through movement must be carried by r1; through is therefore inferred, not read from a marking. Whether left turns are also permitted from r1 cannot be determined: no arrow, and no legible lane-use or turn-prohibition sign faces EB (the median-nose sign is seen from behind). The lane may in fact be a shared left/through lane. Upstream (far view, about 101 m) only one motor lane exists. The second lane is added between the far and mid positions, and r1 continues the original single lane.

evidence: Retained. In the satellite, r2 is about 3.1 m between the thick solid separator and a thinner solid line, with a pavement arrow just behind the stop bar. In both forward views the right motor lane sits between the same solid separator and the line bordering the bicycle lane.
binding: Near view: a large right-turn arrow (curved stem turning right, no straight branch) lies in the lane right of the solid separator, a few metres before the stop bar. Mid view: the word 'ONLY' is painted in the same lane (between the solid separator and the bicycle-lane line), with an arrow-shaped mark beyond it near the stop line in the same lane position. Satellite: a right-turn-shaped arrow inside r2 just behind the stop bar. The three are bound by the same left boundary (the solid separator, which is the satellite's r1/r2 line) and the same right neighbour (the bicycle strip). The arrow plus 'ONLY' supports a dedicated right-turn lane. Imagery is 2020-11 GSV and spring 2021 satellite; the two dates agree.

evidence: Retained. r3 is about 1.4 m between the thin solid line and the right kerb. The satellite shows a green-painted patch inside it at the building-shadow edge. The mid forward view shows a green-painted bicycle lane immediately right of the 'ONLY' lane, separated by a solid white line. In the near view the narrow leaf-covered strip right of the right-turn lane runs to the kerb, and the stop bar extends across it. The strip is too narrow for a motor lane and carries no arrow.
binding: Bound by position: the strip directly right of the right-turn/ONLY lane's right line in all views, and r3 in the satellite. Green paint is observed in the mid view and in the satellite r3 strip. No bicycle symbol is readable near the stop bar (leaves in the near view, tree shadow on the satellite). Upstream (far view) the bicycle lane continues with green paint and a hatched buffer to its right. At the mid position an extra asphalt wedge lies between the green lane and the kerb; it is not a travel lane and has no region.

evidence: Kept. In the satellite this is an asphalt lane about 3.1 m wide, the first lane right of the opposing side (with parked cars). It is bounded on the right by a white lane line and ends at its own set-back stop line. The mid street view shows the same lane as the first lane right of the double yellow centre line, which bends left near the junction as r1 does. The near view's camera stands just left of the double yellow at a transverse stop line right of it, consistent with r1's set-back stop line.
binding: Two left-curving arrows lie inside r1 in the satellite, one near the set-back stop line and one upstream; I re-checked the shapes on the satellite panel. In the mid street view (2020-11) the arrow in the first lane right of the double yellow has its head on the left and its stem hooking toward the camera, a left-turn arrow; this binds to r1 by its position next to the centre line. No arrow combining through and left is seen in either source. The near view shows a building frontage and plaza straight ahead across the cross street and no through roadway. Street views are from 2020-11 and the satellite from spring 2021; the arrows agree.

evidence: Kept. In the satellite this is asphalt about 3.0 m wide between the r1 lane line and the double white line (r3). Its stop bar joins the line in an L just before the crosswalk. The mid street view shows the second lane from the centre line, bounded on the right by a white line with flexible delineator posts.
binding: Two right-curving arrows lie inside r2 in the satellite. The native-pixel detail crop of the mid street view (detail_2) shows the second lane's arrow clearly: a stem hooking down toward the camera at its left end, and a widened arrowhead at its right end. That is a foreshortened right-turn arrow, with no through branch. It binds to r2 as the lane between the left-arrow lane and the post-lined line. The near view shows an L-shaped stop bar and line at upper right ahead of the camera, matching r2's head. Upstream, the far view (113 m) has one travel lane plus kerbside parking; by the mid view (59 m) there are two lanes, with the dividing line dashed nearer the camera. So r2 develops as a right-turn pocket.

evidence: Kept as a separator. In the satellite and in detail_1 it is two closely spaced parallel solid white lines about 0.7 m apart. The mid street view, including detail_2, shows white flexible delineator posts (and an orange one further on) standing along the line right of the right-turn lane. This is a painted, post-lined buffer, not a travel lane.
binding: Bound by position immediately right of the right-turn lane in both satellite and mid street view. Upstream, the far view shows the posts on a hatched buffer at the end of the parking lane.

evidence: Paved strip about 1.65 m wide between the buffer's right line and a further single solid white line. The single line is clearly visible in detail_1, running from near the stop bar diagonally down-left. The irregular light marking inside the strip is still a blur in the native crop: two lobes with no recognisable wheel/rider outline. It cannot be confirmed as a bicycle symbol, and could equally be post bases or debris. In detail_2 the kerbside space beyond the posts reads as one pavement band. A second line cannot be resolved there, so the street view neither confirms nor rules out the r4/r5 split. Too narrow for a car lane.
binding: Satellite only. No marking in the street views can be bound to r4. It may be a separate bicycle lane, part of a wider bicycle facility shared with r5, or extra buffer width.

evidence: Kept. Paved strip about 1.8 m wide between the single solid white line and the right kerb, with the tan sidewalk directly beyond. Detail_1 shows an elongated light marking with a broader leading end pointing in the travel direction, a straight arrow, just upstream of the stop area. No bicycle symbol is visible near it. The mid and far street views show a post-separated kerbside bicycle facility (bike-share dock on the sidewalk beside it; hatched buffer with posts upstream). The near view shows green bicycle-crossing paint beyond the crosswalk on this side. Its width rules out a motor lane.
binding: Bound as the kerbside strip beyond the post-lined buffer, next to the sidewalk. The straight arrow is a bicycle-lane direction marking and does not set motor-vehicle turn permissions, so no motor movement is assigned. Whether r4 and r5 are one facility or two remains unresolved.

evidence: Retained. Uniform asphalt about 3.4 m wide between a faint left edge and the solid white line it shares with r2. It holds two curved pavement arrows and starts at the stop bar. Street view mid shows the same lane: between the raised median kerb and the solid white line, marked 'ONLY' with a turn arrow, running up to the stop line.
binding: Satellite: both arrows in r1 have the stem at the lower right and the head bending to the upper left (driver's left), i.e. left-turn arrows, one near the stop bar and one about 25 m upstream; none has a U-turn hook. Street view mid (2020-11): the leftmost lane between the median kerb and the solid white line carries the word ONLY and, ahead, a wide flat turn arrow. Its perspective width is about twice that of the straight arrow in the next lane, consistent with a left-turn arrow. Same physical anchors in both: median/left limit, the solid line between lanes, the through-arrow lane to its right. The street-view arrow head direction alone is blurry; the satellite arrow shape settles it. The about 6 m unregioned strip left of r1 in the satellite is uniform, dark and shadowed. Street view mid shows the median kerb directly beside the ONLY lane up to the crosswalk, so that strip is most likely the median in shadow, not another lane.

evidence: Retained. Asphalt about 3.4 m wide between two solid white lines, with straight arrows and a car stopped at the stop bar. Street view mid shows the camera's lane between the same two lines with a straight arrow near the stop line.
binding: Satellite: a straight arrow (head forward) in r2 near the stop bar and another upstream; no turn shape is visible in this lane. Street view mid: compact straight arrow in the camera lane near the stop line, between the ONLY lane's solid line and the solid line beside the bicycle strip. No right-turn arrow or right-turn pocket is visible. The near view shows the right kerb and sidewalk running straight past the crosswalk, with no right-hand leg visible. A right turn from this lane is therefore not supported by any marking, but no sign forbidding it was read either. 'through_only' rests on the arrows alone.

evidence: Revised from uncertain to supported. Satellite: a paved strip about 2 m wide between the outer solid white line and the kerb, too narrow for a car lane. Street view near: a green-painted strip along the right kerb up to the crosswalk, i.e. a marked bicycle lane, with a band of older grey asphalt between it and the new black travel-lane asphalt. Street view mid and far: a solid white line with a strip of bicycle-lane width between it and the granite kerb all along the approach.
binding: Bound by order: kerb, then this strip, then the solid white line, then the through lane (r2) in all three street views and in the satellite. The green paint is seen only in the near view (2020-11), on freshly resurfaced pavement. No bicycle symbol is readable in any view. Exactly where the grey buffer band ends and the bicycle lane begins inside r3 is not resolvable.

evidence: r1 (about 2.5 m) is a slightly darker, smooth band between two faint longitudinal edges. Its left edge lines up with the end of the opposing (WB) stop bar and the right edge of the WB turn lane, which has down-pointing arrows. It has no lane paint and no vehicles. The look-back GSV from the WB approach shows a planted grass median with a kerb, a yellow edge line and a row of trees between the WB 'ONLY' turn lane and the EB carriageway. r1 is the only strip of median width in that position. The whole scene is in shadow, so tree trunks and the kerb are not individually resolvable on the satellite.

r2 (about 3.7 m) is uniform asphalt between the median band and a continuous solid white line on its right. It is wide enough for one motor lane, and the crosswalk at the junction end runs across it. In the GSV, beyond the median, one EB travel lane runs along the median before the pair of white lines and the parked vehicles. No arrows are readable on r2 in either image.

r3 (about 1.5 m) lies between two parallel solid white lines that run continuously from the crosswalk to the far end of the section. It sits between the travel strip r2 and the row of parked cars. In the GSV, two parallel white lines separate the EB travel lane from the parked vehicles. The narrow width and position fit a bicycle lane between the travel lane and parking, but no bicycle symbol is legible, so the subtype is not confirmed.

r4 (about 5.9 m) holds a tight bumper-to-bumper row of stationary cars right of the white-line pair, which is a kerbside parking lane. Beyond the cars the crosswalk stops and a smooth, slightly warmer strip runs up to the building faces; this looks like sidewalk or tree lawn rather than carriageway. In the GSV, parked vehicles (a pickup and a Jeep) stand at the EB far kerb, with grass and sidewalk behind them. No travel-lane marking is visible in r4.

r1's left edge follows a continuous bright longitudinal line, read as the centre line. On the other side of it are the opposing approach's lanes, whose turn arrows point toward the junction. The left ~3.5 m of r1 is uniform asphalt with no parked objects: a SB travel lane leaving the junction. About 64% of the way across, a faint longitudinal line separates it from the right ~2 m. That right part holds a row of three cars parked end to end along the kerb, so it is a parking lane, not travel pavement. Beyond the kerb are tree-shadowed sidewalk/plaza, brick paving and buildings. The reverse look-back street view shows the same arrangement on this side of the double yellow line: one travel lane, then a solid white edge line, then cars parked at the kerb, then the sidewalk with café seating. r1 is therefore supported as a travel facility, but it covers one motor-vehicle lane plus a parking strip; only about 3.5 m of its 5.5 m width is travel lane. Most of it lies in building shadow.

Continuous grey asphalt starting just beyond the crosswalk. Its left side is the kerb of a raised median island (with a shelter or bench structure and a planter at the island nose). Its right side is the left line of a painted buffer. Profiles across the strip show uniform pavement about 4.6-5 m wide with no lane line inside it, so it reads as one wide general-traffic lane, not two. The upper part lies in a building shadow, but the pavement continues. In the reverse GSV, the carriageway across the planted median also shows a single wide lane left of a two-line buffer.

About 1.3 m between two parallel solid white lines, with diagonal hatch marks painted between them at regular intervals along the whole strip. This is a painted buffer separating the travel lane from the kerbside bicycle lane, not a travel facility. In the reverse GSV, the far-side carriageway shows the same two-line buffer with a white flexible delineator post.

Paved strip about 1.9-2.0 m wide between the buffer's right line and the kerb. Beyond the kerb lies a light sidewalk with a row of round reddish planters at its edge, granite-edged tree pits and further sidewalk. Near the lower part of the strip there is a white arrow pointing in the direction of travel with a glyph behind it consistent with a bicycle-lane symbol, though too small to resolve fully. The arrow is a direction marking for the bike lane, not a turn arrow. The width, the buffer and the marking fit a buffered bicycle lane; it is too narrow for a car lane. The reverse GSV shows the same kerbside strip beyond the buffer on the far-side carriageway.
